item.title: Apatang signs FY 2027 budget, issues broad vetoes

item.content:encoded:
CNMI Gov. David M. Apatang on Monday signed Public Law 24‑40, the Fiscal Year 2027 budget, after a five‑day partial government shutdown that began when the administration said it needed additional time to review the Legislature’s spending plan.

In a letter to lawmakers, Apatang said the budget reached his office “just hours prior to the opening of the new fiscal year,” leaving insufficient time for review and prompting the temporary halt in government operations.

The new law sets a projected annual revenue target of about $152.8 million, including $47.7 million in earmarks and $100.7 million allocated across all branches and government instrumentalities.

Apatang approved the overall spending plan but vetoed several provisions he said were unfunded, legally inconsistent, or fiscally unsustainable. He rejected a mandate requiring minimum compensation levels and 64‑hour workweeks, saying the measure would widen the Commonwealth’s budget gap by roughly $3.3 million. He also disapproved of language restricting furloughs and guaranteeing full benefits despite reduced work hours, arguing that agencies must retain flexibility during austerity.

The governor struck a proposed salary cap tied to his July 1 budget submission, calling it a violation of separation of powers. He also vetoed requirements for immediate transfers of FEMA‑reimbursable funds to municipal treasuries, noting that the Department of Finance does not control FEMA drawdowns. Several Public School System funding directives were rejected after Apatang said they front‑loaded spending and created an unfunded mandate of more than $7 million. Additional vetoes affected the Department of Public Lands, the Office of the Attorney General, and other operational provisions he said conflicted with existing law or lacked a sustainable funding source.

Apatang said his administration will implement proportionate budget reductions and forthcoming work‑hour adjustments to align spending with available revenues. With his signature, the budget becomes law and agencies are preparing to resume normal operations.

item.title: One crane repaired, returned to service at port of Guam
item.description: One of the port’s three cranes damaged by high winds Friday night has been repaired and placed back into service Monday afternoon. The Port Authority of Guam said Gantry Crane 4 is operational and was used Monday to load 10 refrigerated containers onto a Matson barge bound for Saipan. It will also be used to unload a ship arriving Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
One of the port’s three cranes damaged by high winds Friday night has been repaired and placed back into service Monday afternoon.

The Port Authority of Guam said Gantry Crane 4 is operational and was used Monday to load 10 refrigerated containers onto a Matson barge bound for Saipan. It will also be used to unload a ship arriving Tuesday.

Gantry Crane 5 has been returned to the rail system but will require repairs, inspection and recertification before returning to service. Crews are working to return Gantry Crane 6 to the rail system.

The port is also trying to rent a mobile crane to help with vessel operations.

Friday night’s incident occurred when Gantry Crane 6 became dislodged from its secured position and traveled approximately 1,000 feet along the crane rail system before hitting Gantry Cranes 5 and 4. No injuries were reported, but all three cranes were damaged.

Gantry Crane 6 had been locked in position and secured at the time.

The Port Authority said gauges on the crane recorded winds of about 100 mph during the incident. The Port has not characterized the incident as either a procedural failure or mechanical malfunction as the technical assessment remains ongoing.

The assessments will help determine what effect, if any, Friday night’s incident has had on the remaining service lives of Gantries 5 and 6.

item.title: Coast Guard clears Saipan harbor for full commercial operations
item.description: The U.S. Coast Guard has reopened the Port of Saipan to all commercial vessel traffic and cargo operations after determining that hazardous conditions from Typhoon Choi‑Wan no longer pose a threat. Captain of the Port J.S. Worst announced the reset to Port Heavy Weather Condition Whiskey at 7 a.m. Monday, allowing business activity to resume without restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Coast Guard has reopened the Port of Saipan to all commercial vessel traffic and cargo operations after determining that hazardous conditions from Typhoon Choi‑Wan no longer pose a threat.

Captain of the Port J.S. Worst announced the reset to Port Heavy Weather Condition Whiskey at 7 a.m. Monday, allowing business activity to resume without restrictions.

Choi-Wan strengthened to 145 mph Sunday evening as it continued moving north away from the Mariana Islands,

In a notice issued to shipping agents, vessel masters, and facility operators, Worst said the port is “hereby open to all commercial traffic and cargo operations without restrictions,” marking a significant step in Saipan’s post‑storm recovery. However, the Port of Tinian remains closed to maritime traffic until further assessment.

The Coast Guard cautioned mariners to navigate carefully when entering or departing Saipan’s harbor. While no major obstructions were found, aids to navigation may have shifted and shoaling could have occurred during the typhoon. Mariners are encouraged to report any discrepancies via VHF channels 16 or 22A or by calling the Sector Guam Command Center.

Commercially regulated facilities may still face operational limitations, and the Coast Guard urged shipping agents and operators to coordinate directly with terminal managers to ensure safe cargo handling and vessel movements.

Questions regarding heavy weather conditions and port status may be directed to the USCG Forces Micronesia/Sector Guam Prevention Department.

item.title: Is our fate pre-destined? A new 'East of Eden' adaptation asks again

item.content:encoded:
As John Steinbeck wrote it, East of Eden is a sprawling, ambitious, provocative novel, spanning from the Civil War to the end of World War I. Its primary characters include an Irish immigrant family and a Chinese loner, several generations of feuding brothers and an evil and manipulative young girl who matures into an even more evil and manipulative woman. And through it all runs the author's central question: Are we pre-destined to a particular fate and disposition, or can free will overcome?

The movie version, produced in the 1950s and adapted with Steinbeck's input, chopped off the first three-quarters of the book. Director Elia Kazan opens with Cal Trask, one of two very dissimilar brothers, hunting down his mother, who abandoned the family right after her twins were born. Cal and his brother, Aron, are like the biblical Cain and Abel — one is good by nature, the other evil — but in the movie, Cal is played with palpable charisma by James Dean.

The next version of East of Eden arrived in 1981. The six-hour ABC miniseries used the extra time to include more characters and stories neglected in the film. The Hamiltons, the Irish family, are given lots of room to develop, as is Lee, the Chinese caretaker, who is much wiser than he originally appears. Most of all, that miniseries brought the character of Cathy to dead center. As played by Jane Seymour , she was a force of nature — and of pure evil, who, after giving birth to twins she didn't want, would shoot her husband and abandon her babies.

I've revisited these earlier versions to put into a fuller context just what Zoe Kazan has done in revising, and remaking, the story first brought to screen by her grandfather. This new Netflix miniseries, at about seven hours, is slightly longer than the older one — but it basically eliminates the Irish American family, so it can't claim to be more complete. It also can't claim to be the first to focus on the feminist perspective, because the ABC version certainly did that. The new version, though, explores even more fully the transition of Cathy, the young girl, to Kate, the prostitute.

Florence Pugh , as Kate, is given more justification for her actions. She's also given more voice: Instead of Steinbeck providing narration about Kate and her childhood, this new East of Eden has Kate supply it herself. Which she does while listening to a lecture by the man she's about to target.

Pugh's portrayal of Kate, even at the end, is more glamorous than in the previous versions, which showed Kate as older and arthritic. But the drama is unchanged, and many of the confrontation scenes, even ones without violence, are uncomfortably intense. Netflix allows for more sex scenes and nudity, so there's lots of both. But most of these are staged as almost the opposite of erotic: either matter-of-factly, or with one or both parties taking part unwillingly or unenthusiastically. On the night Cathy marries her husband Adam, played by Christopher Abbott, she leaves his bed, and slips into the next room — and into the bed of Adam's brother, Charles, who's understandably startled.

Pugh, like Seymour before her, deserves the spotlight here, and fills it. But watch, also, for Hoon Lee as the family's Chinese manservant and Martha Plimpton as Kate's madam. They're excellent, too. And best of all, this new East of Eden hammers home Steinbeck's primary theme — and suggests, after all the deaths and misery, a potentially happy ending.

item.title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84

item.content:encoded:
Dennis Hastert, whose political legacy as Congress' longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.

Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.

When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.

In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP's poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton's impeachment trial.

After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.

His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert's alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.

During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.

The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.

Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.

Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.

At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a "serial child molester." A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his "dark secret" from adolescence.

In his own statement, Hastert said he was "deeply ashamed" and admitted that he "mistreated" some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.

The public knew nothing about Hastert's past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections.

Hastert's path to the speaker's office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.

Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.

"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."

Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.

As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert's aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.

"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.

Hastert's journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.

In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.

Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.

In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.

Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.

He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.

Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master's in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.

In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert's indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.

Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.

Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

item.title: Ayad Akhtar's 'The Radiance' addresses provocative subjects head-on

item.content:encoded:
Ayad Akhtar does not shy from lightning rod subjects.

As a writer, he repeatedly sticks his neck out in provocative, gripping theatrical plays, including Disgraced, winner of the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and novels, including his second, Homeland Elegies , widely hailed as a best book of 2020. His work exposes the fissures of American racial, political and economic identity, and picks at the fraying seams of a country he regards as stressed by a degradation of democracy and capitalist rapaciousness in all walks of life (including financial, political and medical). His writing gets people talking and thinking — and manages to inflame Muslims and non-Muslims alike.

Akhtar's third novel The Radiance is set during the Covid pandemic in a predominantly white upstate New York town "where it's not unusual to see a Confederate flag." Like Homeland Elegies, its autofictional narrator shares the author's name and many of his biographical details — including his birth in America to secular, Pakistani-born doctors, and his career highlights — although not necessarily his actual experiences and thoughts.

The novel recounts what happens after the narrator is knocked off his bicycle by a hit-and-run driver in a pickup truck on a deserted country road. In a nutshell, he loses his spleen and his anger. In the "ambrosial afterglow" of what seems to have been a deliberate hit, the narrator Ayad's perceptions intensify, as if "there's light everywhere" and his "emotions are all in primary colors." He's frequently moved to tears by everyday occurrences such as sunsets. He likens his new sense of harmony, beauty, and completeness to what Dostoyevsky felt after his epileptic seizures.

But the narrator, like the author, is a cerebral, hyperarticulate writer who is thrown when he can't find the words to convey his new heightened, paranormal sensations. He worries how this profound change will impact his writing. He talks to doctors and local friends about this, including a fictional couple central to his story: a professor of Comparative Literature named Lucie Neroponte and her husband Stanford Lewis, a black doctor and poet of some renown.

Although the convalescent narrator has lost his libido in the accident, he is increasingly enamored with Lucie, and looks forward to her soup-bearing visits. Lucie rails about her students' "near-total inability to concentrate," and worse, "having to bear the moralizing brunt of some perceived breach of their pronouns or politics." She declares scathingly: "what these students are absolutely not is anything remotely interesting." The sole exception, she says, is a diligent young woman from Idaho named Susan Yi.

Among its many concerns, The Radiance addresses problems in higher education, including the erosion of attention spans, critical acuity, mental resilience and flexibility in a generation pelted by misinformation on the internet. The novel also considers how the #MeToo movement changed attitudes toward sexual harassment, abuse, and rape.

Around 2000, Ayad tells us, Lucie published a long personal essay called "Growing Pains," about an affair she had in 1990 with a married professor more than 30 years her senior. Lucie wrote that she was a 20-year-old college junior when she seduced him . She candidly described their sacrilegious sex in the church sacristy and library stacks — all of which she found "intoxicating (until it wasn't)." Her essay made a splash. But after #MeToo went viral in 2017, the narrator recounts, "her unrepentant eroticization of a relationship no longer deemed licit" cost Lucie tenure at a prestigious university and cast a shadow over her brilliant academic career. She had landed at a small college in the Hudson Valley.

Yet despite her misgivings, Lucie urges Ayad to fill a vacancy in the creative writing department by teaching a course in autofiction. Susan Yi joins his class. He's soon in hot water, after his writing prompts lead to sexualized content, including a story that suggests that Susan may have had or been groomed for an affair with Lucie.

The Radiance is told in post-radiance hindsight from the narrator's notes, with much commentary along the way. It is a discursive, multi-layered construct that's sometimes a head-scratcher. Academics are run out of town, yet white supremacist arsonists and hit-and-run drivers go scot-free. The novel includes reflections on the writing life and "the self-shaped knot" it ties writers into (particularly self-involved writers), as well as detailed sessions with a psychiatrist trying to untangle changes in the narrator's personality. The late classicist and political philosopher Allan Bloom, author of The Closing of the American Mind , a popular critique of American higher education, figures in Lucie's story, as does Plato's Phaedrus .

In one of the novel's most powerful episodes, Ayad learns from a first cousin, the daughter of his father's long-estranged brother, the root cause of his father's lifelong aberrant behavior: Multiple acts of brutality the two brothers were subjected to as young boys in Peshawar. This revelation, seemingly a tangential footnote to Homeland Elegies , indirectly yet deftly highlights the long tail of trauma that figures in The Radiance. In his first class session, Ayad tells his students that "convincing fiction ... was a chain of linked actions — believable to the extent they were seen as probable, absorbing to the extent they were felt as necessary." Akhtar rattles a lot of chains in this thought-provoking novel. I'm not convinced they all pass this test, but enough do to add up to a profound reading experience.

item.title: Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone
item.description: KYIV, Ukraine — The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I. Yet straddling this front line is the kill zone , dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.
item.content:encoded:
KYIV, Ukraine — The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I.

Yet straddling this front line is the kill zone , dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.

"This kill zone is a belt of territory which is full of Russian drones, Russian mines and also artillery. It's nonstop reconnaissance and surveillance," said Ukraine's Sr. Lt. Taras Myshak, the spokesman for Ukraine's 59th Separate Assault Brigade. He spoke with NPR on Zoom, just a few miles from the front line in eastern Ukraine.

Ukraine has a similar arsenal threatening the Russian forces that are dug in on the other side of the line.

The most important thing to know about the kill zone is that any sign of movement — just sticking your head out of a foxhole for fresh air — can get you noticed, and attacked, by the drones constantly buzzing overhead.

Myshak says even routine movements, like rotating troops in and out of this zone, is a nightmare.

"Not far from where we are talking today, we have a group that moved through the kill zone, and they will walk four hours just to go 1 kilometer," he said. "Because all the time they hear the drone, and they have to hide and wait. Then the drone passes, and they can move."

Nightfall doesn't make it any safer to move because the drones have thermal cameras that detect body heat and make it even harder to hide.

"In the night, it's even more dangerous," he said.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it advanced rapidly in conventional fashion with large columns of troops in armored vehicles. Later that fall, Ukraine's counteroffensive drove the Russians back in some places.

Since then, the two armies have settled in, and the front line has moved only incrementally, mostly with limited gains by Russia. This line now stretches more than 700 miles. On either side of the line, the kill zone is a band roughly 10 to 20 miles wide and dominated by drones.

"The kill zone is basically a product of drone warfare," said Rob Lee, a U.S. Marine veteran who now lives in Ukraine and monitors the war for the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.

Because Ukraine has far fewer troops and relies heavily on drones, it has a remarkably small presence on the front line.

Lee said that in many places, Ukraine has fewer than 10 soldiers per mile, in small groups, spaced out hundreds of yards apart.

"Those infantrymen are maybe two positions where it's two to four people," said Lee. "They're underground for the most part. They're trying to remain hidden."

These troops are not really trying to hold back advancing Russian soldiers, he added. They act more as spotters, relaying Russian movements to Ukrainian drone operators behind the front lines, who then track down the Russian intruders from the air.

Lee says the front line is so saturated with drones that it's virtually impossible for either side to pull together a large ground force without being detected and drawing fire.

Military vehicles like tanks and armored personnel carriers are even easier to spot and attack.

"Because of such a high density of drones, it became very difficult to bring vehicles near the front line at all," he said.

Ukraine had no real drone industry at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the country will make 10 million this year.

Russia has ramped up its own drone production. It's expected to make more than 7 million this year, including jet-powered aircraft that are often evading Ukraine's defenses.

When Dima Putiata joined Ukraine's military four years ago, he knew nothing about drones and didn't think this was a manly way to wage war.

"When I saw that we have drones, I was not smart enough. I said, 'No, we don't need to have it. Let's fight like men.' I was a little bit maybe romantic in this way," said Putiata.

In addition to skeptics like Putiata, few Ukrainian troops were trained to use these new weapons.

"No one had drone operators," he recalled. "It's just, 'Oh, you're a driver? You can use it.' Or, 'Oh, can I use a drone? You can try.'"

By the time he left the military in May, Putiata, a sergeant, was commanding 26 drone crews in and around the kill zone in northeastern Ukraine.

Both sides have rapidly embraced the technology even if they don't know where it's headed next, he said.

"They understand how to use it here and right now, maybe not really understanding how to use it in the future," he noted. "My point is, you just need to keep going and adapting."

Two years ago, Ukraine became the first country to establish drones as an independent branch of its military.

This innovation now includes the widespread use of ground drones, which look like trollies and perform a wide range of tasks that have become too dangerous for troops.
